newsitem.title: USA: US 30-yr mortgage rate falls fifth consecutive wk.
newsitem.headline: US 30-yr mortgage rate falls fifth consecutive wk.

text.p: The average interest rate on U.S. 30-year fixed-rate mortgages fell to 7.53 percent in the week ending November 22, a fifth consecutive weekly decline, the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp said Thursday.
Freddie Mac said the 30-year rate has not been lower since it stood at 7.38 percent in the week ended March 8, 1996. Last week's 30-year rate was 7.59 percent.
Fifteen-year loans also fell a fifth consecutive week to an average 7.06 percent, the lowest since a rate of 6.87 percent in the March 8 week. Last week's 15-year rate averaged 7.11 percent.
Adjustable-rate mortgages inched downward to an average 5.48 percent, the lowest since a rate of 5.40 percent in the week ended March 8. Last week's ARM averaged 5.52 percent.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 7.35 percent, the 15-year 6.85 percent, and the ARM 5.61 percent.

"Since there is little fear this week that inflation will rise or the Fed will raise rates anytime soon, interest rates declined slightly for the fifth week in a row," Robert Van Order, Freddie Mac chief economist, said.
"Because the overall economy is rather slow, we would expect interest rates to hover around 7.5 percent for the foreseeable future," he said.
On Tuesday the Commerce Department said U.S. October housing starts fell 5.1 percent to an annual rate of 1.366 million.
The Federal Open Market Committee decided at its November 13 meeting to leave interest rates unchanged.

In the latest week, Freddie Mac said lenders charged an average 1.8 percent in fees and points on 30-year loans and 1.4 percent on ARM loans, las, both unchanged from the previous week. They charged 1.7 percent on 15-year mortgages, down from 1.8 percent in the previous week.
